source.title: Attention Output SAEs Improve Circuit Analysis

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE reconstruction error matters to behavior and circuit-score analyses, using SAE reconstruction, error ablation, and variance attribution rather than the target claim's linear-predictability and cross-size measurements.
record.gate_note: The post evaluates replacing attention outputs with SAE reconstructions and reports results for ablating the error term and measuring its contribution to an attention-score decomposition. It does not compare SAE errors with random errors of the same size, test linear predictability from input activations, or compare error patterns across SAE sizes. The noising experiments and most feature/circuit analyses do not measure the target claim's error properties.
record.test_reason: Splicing attention-output SAE reconstructions into GPT-2 Small drops the error term, and the post measures IOI logit difference and KL. It also zero-ablates the error term and measures the error's share of attention-score variance. These results bear directly on V5 in a circuit-analysis setting. No version other than V5 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors add that SAEs gave novel IOI insights (the 'and'-based positional signal) and enabled recursive DFA. Later-layer SAEs were 'pretty useless', which they hope better or bigger SAEs will fix.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates SAE-reconstruction effects on IOI and circuit-score analyses; does not use the target study's linear prediction, per-token scaling, or cross-size error comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported reconstruction effects differ by layer and head-role cross-section: early-middle layers are described as sufficient, while layer 0 and later layers show substantial problems.
record.problems: The relevant outcomes are mostly qualitative, with no separate numerical values for layers or head-role groups. The post does not compare SAE reconstruction errors to random errors of matched size, and the circuit-variance result is limited to 100 prompts and one analyzed path.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly relevant results omitted. Noising experiments, feature interpretations, and recursive-DFA examples do not measure the versions of the claim about SAE error.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the error from input activations was not measured.
No cross-size or per-token error-norm analysis.
No comparison of SAE error with random errors of matched norm.
No decomposition of the error into linear and nonlinear parts.
Steering is not tested, and no circuit other than IOI is evaluated quantitatively. MLP and residual SAEs are not evaluated by splicing.
No comparison of architectures or training objectives. The authors only speculate that better or bigger SAEs may fix the later layers.

missing.what: In the RDFA 'Dave' example, the error term dominates the resid_pre attribution at the 'is' source position for feature 10.14709. This is a qualitative case where the error carries much of the attributed signal.
missing.locator: Example: Retrieving "Dave" using recursive attention attribution

missing.what: The splicing figure also compares each layer's SAE splicing with mean-ablating that layer's attention output (ABC distribution). This gives a scale for how much behaviour is lost. No row records it.
missing.locator: Evaluating our SAEs for IOI Circuit Analysis, first figure

record.verdict_notes: All V5-relevant results are qualitative readings of figures, with no numbers except r11 (15% vs 62%). The layer-dependent pattern is the key point: the error matters in layer 0 and late layers but not in layers 1-6. The authors attribute the late-layer failure to rare, name-specific features, which is speculation and was not tested (relevant to V4 and V6).

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of the error vector is linearly predictable from the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability, whether larger and smaller SAEs fail on the same contexts, and whether error persists with scale.
The post measures effects of SAE reconstruction but does not compare them with random errors of the same size.
Whether the linear component represents unlearned features and whether the nonlinear component resists further dictionary learning.
Tests concern IOI behavior and one attention-score decomposition, not the share of behavior lost across other circuits or analyses such as steering.
No comparison of SAE training objectives, architectures, shrinkage, dead latents, or end-to-end training.
